title: ES modules: splitting code into files
goal: Organise JavaScript into modules with import and export, in the browser and in Node.

concepts: Why modules: each file has its own scope, explicit dependencies
Named exports vs default export, and import { a as b }
<script type="module"> in the browser (deferred automatically, needs a server)
ES modules in Node: "type": "module" in package.json or .mjs files
Module structure: data, logic (pure functions), and UI/DOM in separate files
CommonJS (require/module.exports) vs ES modules

build.task: Refactor your Day 41 to-do app into modules in day49/: storage.js (load/save with try/catch), todos.js (pure functions: addTodo(list, text) returns a new list, toggleTodo, editTodo, deleteTodo, filterTodos, countActive), ui.js (render and DOM helpers only), and main.js (wires events to state and render). Use named exports. Then create day49/test-todos.mjs that imports todos.js in Node and runs at least 10 checks on the pure functions. Serve the page with VS Code Live Server or npx serve (modules don't work from file://).
acceptance: 4 modules with clear responsibilities; todos.js has no DOM or localStorage code
todos.js functions are pure and return new arrays
main.js is the only file that knows about both state and the DOM
test-todos.mjs runs with node and passes 10+ checks
App works exactly as before when served over http

hints: If the browser console says 'CORS' or 'Failed to load module script' you opened the file directly. Use Live Server or run npx serve day49 and open the printed URL.
Import paths need the file extension in the browser: import { addTodo } from './todos.js'.
To import todos.js in Node, it must be an ES module. Name the test file .mjs, and either add a package.json with "type": "module" in day49/ or rename todos.js to todos.mjs.
proof: Commit with day49/ files and the test output.

explainBack.q: Why did you keep todos.js free of DOM and localStorage code? What did that let you do?
lookFor: pure logic is testable in Node
UI can change without touching logic

explainBack.q: What's the difference between a named export and a default export?
lookFor: named: imported with braces by exact name
default: one per module, any import name

lastHintExplanation: Keeping todos.js pure (no DOM, no storage) means you can import and test it in Node without a browser, and change the UI freely. Named exports are imported in braces by their exact names, and a file can have many. A default export is one per file and can be imported under any name.

predict.q: a.js: export let count = 1; export function inc() { count++ }. main.js: import { count, inc } from './a.js'; inc(); console.log(count)
predict.why: ES module imports are live bindings: they reflect the exporter's current value.

node_modules and package-lock.json (commit the lock file, ignore node_modules)
Semantic versioning: ^1.2.3 means compatible updates

Importing an npm package in browser code

Check git status before committing. If you see hundreds of files in node_modules, your .gitignore isn't in the right folder.

explainBack.q: Why is node_modules ignored but package-lock.json committed?
lookFor: node_modules is huge and can be rebuilt with npm install
so everyone/servers install the same versions

explainBack.q: What does npm run build produce, and why don't we deploy the src folder directly?
lookFor: resolves npm imports for the browser

lastHintExplanation: node_modules can be recreated at any time with npm install, so it's not committed; package-lock.json records the exact versions installed so every machine gets the same tree. npm run build bundles your modules and npm packages into a few optimised files in dist/. Browsers can't resolve 'date-fns' on their own, and many small files load slowly.

predict.q: package.json has "date-fns": "^3.6.0". Which version could npm install?
predict.why: ^ allows minor and patch updates within the same major version.

title: Classes, prototypes and custom errors
goal: Model things with classes when it helps, understand what's happening underneath, and throw meaningful errors.

concepts: class syntax: constructor, methods, getters
Private fields with #name
Inheritance with extends and super()
Under the hood: prototypes and the prototype chain (just the idea)
Custom error classes: class ValidationError extends Error
When to use a class vs plain objects and functions

build.task: In day51/, write wallet.js: class Wallet with a private #balance and #transactions, methods deposit(amount, note), spend(amount, note, category), a getter balance, and history({ category }) returning a copy. Throw a custom ValidationError for invalid amounts (not a positive finite number) and InsufficientFundsError for overspending, each with a helpful message and extra fields. Create class SavingsWallet extends Wallet that refuses to go below a minimumBalance. Write 12+ checks, including checks that the right error class is thrown (use instanceof). Finish with a comment block: when would you NOT use a class?
acceptance: #balance and #transactions can't be accessed from outside (prove it in a check or comment)
ValidationError and InsufficientFundsError extend Error and set name
SavingsWallet uses extends and super, and overrides spend correctly
history() returns a copy; changing it doesn't affect the wallet
12+ passing checks including instanceof error checks
Comment explaining when plain functions/objects are a better choice

hints: class InsufficientFundsError extends Error { constructor(needed, available) { super(`Need ₹${needed}, have ₹${available}`); this.name = 'InsufficientFundsError'; this.needed = needed; } }
Testing a throw: try { w.spend(1e9) ; check('throws', false, true) } catch (e) { check('right error', e instanceof InsufficientFundsError, true) }.
In SavingsWallet.spend, check the minimum first, then call super.spend(amount, note, category).

lookFor: truly private, can't be changed from outside
all changes go through methods that validate

explainBack.q: Why create custom error classes instead of throwing plain strings?

lastHintExplanation: #private fields can't be read or written outside the class, so every change goes through methods that validate it and the balance can never become invalid. Custom error classes let callers tell errors apart with instanceof and carry extra data (like the amount needed), and they keep a stack trace, which a thrown string doesn't.

predict.q: class A { #x = 1 } const a = new A(); console.log(a.#x)
predict.why: Accessing a private field outside the class is a syntax error.

predict.q: class E extends Error {} const e = new E('x'); console.log(e instanceof Error, e instanceof E)
predict.why: E inherits from Error, so it's an instance of both.

explainBack.q: Why might you store money in paise instead of rupees with decimals?
Walk through your module structure and what each file is allowed to know about.

lastHintExplanation: Computers store decimals in binary, so 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. Money in integer paise is exact, and you only format it as ₹ for display. Keeping pure logic, storage and UI in separate modules means each part can be tested and changed on its own.

predict.why: Binary floating point can't represent 0.1 and 0.2 exactly; the sum is 0.30000000000000004.

explainBack.q: Why do you update an existing Chart.js instance instead of creating a new chart on each render?
lookFor: creating new charts on same canvas causes errors/duplicates/memory leaks

explainBack.q: What does Vite's base option do and why did GitHub Pages need it?

Creating a new one on every render stacks charts, leaks memory and throws 'Canvas is already in use', so keep one instance and update its data. build.task: Machine-coding practice (90 minutes, no notes for the first 60): in jobready-journey/day54/, build a 'Quiz app' with plain JS modules. Fetch 10 questions from https://opentdb.com/api.php?amount=10&type=multiple (decode HTML entities safely, e.g. via a <textarea> or DOMParser), shuffle answers, show one question at a time with a 15-second timer per question, score, and a results screen with what you got wrong and a 'Play again' button. hints: Plan states first: 'loading' → 'question' → 'results'. One render() that switches on state.
Decoding entities like " safely: const doc = new DOMParser().parseFromString(text, 'text/html'); return doc.documentElement.textContent;
Timer: clear the previous interval every time you show a new question, or timers will stack up.
proof: Links to the checkpoint commit and the final commit.

explainBack.q: What did you look up after the checkpoint and why didn't it stick?
How did you make sure the timer of the previous question didn't keep running?
lookFor: clearInterval before starting a new one / on answer

lastHintExplanation: The quiz is a small state machine: loading, question and results, with one render() that draws the current state. Each question starts a new interval, so you must clearInterval the old one first, or intervals stack and the clock speeds up. Decode HTML entities with DOMParser and insert the result with textContent so API text can't inject markup.
